en: Theragāthā 14.2 Cuddasakanipāta, First Chapter [The verse of the Elder] named Sānu: "Having abandoned all sensual pleasures, having crossed over the flood, I dwell with a mind well-liberated, free from craving. My mind is not attached to anything; I am one who has reached the further shore. The Elder Sānu was thus addressed by the Blessed One: "Monk, you have been born into a family of great wealth; why do you live as a monk? Then the Venerable Sānu, being questioned by the Blessed One, spoke these verses: "I am not one for whom wealth is dear; I have no longing for the household life. I have seen the peril in sensual pleasures; Therefore, I have gone forth into homelessness. "Your father and mother, O monk, Wept as they sent you away. How did you go forth, O monk, Without their permission? "My parents, O Blessed One, Wept as they sent me away. But I went forth with their permission; I am one who has reached the further shore. "Your father and mother, O monk, Wept as they sent you away. How did you go forth, O monk, Without their permission? "My parents, O Blessed One, Wept as they sent me away. The Verses of Godatta Thera:
“Just as a noble thoroughbred horse,
when yoked to the burden, endures the weight of that burden;”
Just as one who is overwhelmed by an excessive load cannot pass through the battle,
so too those who are satiated with wisdom [do not transcend].
Just as the ocean is not filled by water,
so do others not despise them;
for the noble Dhamma indeed protects living beings.
Falling under the power of time at the appointed hour,
and subject to the cycle of repeated existence,
human beings undergo suffering.
Therein young men grieve:
those elevated by the nature of pleasure,
and those fallen by the nature of suffering.
By means of duality fools are slain,
they who do not see things as they truly are;
and those who [perceive] pleasure in what is suffering—
Having transcended the seamstress in the midst,
you stand like a city gatepost—
neither raised nor depressed.
Neither in gain nor in loss,
neither in fame nor in reputation,
neither in blame nor in praise.
They are neither in suffering nor in pleasure;
they are unstained in all things,
like a drop of water on a lotus leaf.
The wise are happy everywhere,
undefeated in all circumstances.
Even that which is not gained through the Dhamma—
Unrighteous gain is inferior;
righteous loss is better than unrighteous gain.
The fame of those with little wisdom and the ill-repute of the wise—
of the wise, ill-repute is indeed better.
There is no fame for those of little wisdom.
Both the praise from the foolish and the censure from the wise—
It is better for the wise to be censured than to be praised by fools;
and [better] than sensual pleasure.
There is suffering in solitude;
yet the suffering of solitude is better than the pleasure consisting of sensual desires.
Between life by unrighteous means and death by righteous means,
death through righteousness is better.
And whatever unrighteousness one might live for;
those who have abandoned desire and anger,
whose minds are peaceful regarding existence and non-existence;
They wander in the world unattached;
for them there is nothing dear or undear.
Having cultivated the factors of enlightenment, they move through the world.
Having attained the faculties and the powers,
they reach supreme peace and,
with taints extinguished, attain final Nibbāna.
… Godatta Thera … The Cuddasaka-nipāta is finished.
Herein is the summary verse (uddāna):
Revata and Godatta—
these two elders possessed great supernormal power;
[they appear] in the fourteenth nipāta.
"Twenty-eight verses."
